title: Redis unavailable makes EVERY request 500 — including /healthz, /readyz and the /admin/system-mode recovery lever
what: SystemModeMiddleware is mounted on '*'. Its ALWAYS_PASS branch — the one whose comment says 'infra probes keep working ... an operator never locks themselves out of the lever they need to pull to recover' — still executes `req.systemMode = await this.modes.resolveGlobal()` BEFORE calling next(). resolveGlobal() calls readCache(), which does a bare `await this.redis.client.get(key)` with no try/catch, and RedisService constructs ioredis with `enableOfflineQueue: false`. So when Redis is not reachable the GET throws synchronously ("Stream isn't writeable and enableOfflineQueue options is false"), the middleware rejects, and the global exception filter turns it into a 500 — for every path, bypassed or not.
impact: A Redis restart, OOM, or a wrong REDIS_URL takes the whole platform down rather than degrading it. Every library gets 500s. The liveness probe cannot say 'alive but degraded', /readyz cannot say which dependency is down, and /admin/system-mode — the documented lever for putting the platform into maintenance and recovering — also 500s, so the operator has no in-band recovery path. Redis in this stack is a single container with appendonly on and no maxmemory; a restart is a routine event.
evidence: EXECUTED. Booted the API (NODE_ENV=production, live audit Postgres) with REDIS_URL=redis://127.0.0.1:6399 (nothing listening). `curl /healthz` → HTTP 500 `{"statusCode":500,"error":"InternalServerError",...,"supportCode":"AYLXKPI6"}`; `curl /readyz` → HTTP 500. The logged stack is exactly: `Error: Stream isn't writeable and enableOfflineQueue options is false ... at SystemModeService.readCache (system-mode.service.ts:232:41) at SystemModeService.resolveGlobal (system-mode.service.ts:44:31) at SystemModeMiddleware.use (system-mode.middleware.ts:100:41)`. With Redis up and only Postgres unreachable, /healthz stays 200 and /readyz returns 503 — confirming Redis, not Postgres, is the single point of total failure.
fix: As stated, PLUS the same try/catch on TenantResolverService.readCache/writeCache (tenant-resolver.service.ts:94-108) — otherwise tenant routes still 500 with Redis down.
verification: RE-EXECUTED independently. Booted apps/api under NODE_ENV=production against the live audit Postgres with REDIS_URL=redis://127.0.0.1:6399 (nothing listening). Results: GET /healthz -> 500 {"supportCode":"5BZQGXX6"}, GET /readyz -> 500, GET /admin/system-mode -> 500. The logged stack is verbatim the one claimed: "Stream isn't writeable and enableOfflineQueue options is false ... at SystemModeService.readCache (system-mode.service.ts:232:41) at SystemModeService.resolveGlobal (:44:31) at SystemModeMiddleware.use (system-mode.middleware.ts:100:41)". Code re-read and matches: middleware.ts:96-101 executes `req.systemMode = await this.modes.resolveGlobal()` INSIDE the ALWAYS_PASS branch before next(); service.ts:231-233 readCache does a bare `await this.redis.client.get(key)`; redis.service.ts:25 sets `enableOfflineQueue: false`. Searched for a guard that would prevent it and found NONE — the global filter (http-exception.filter.ts:74) turns the rejection into a 500. Control test: with Redis up and only the control DB dead, /healthz stayed 200 and /readyz returned 503, so Redis is uniquely the total-failure dependency. ADDITIONAL, not in the original: TenantResolverService.readCache (apps/api/src/tenancy/tenant-resolver.service.ts:94-96) has the identical unguarded `this.redis.client.get` — so a fix confined to SystemModeService still leaves every /t/<slug>/* request 500ing on a Redis outage. Severity blocker upheld: a routine Redis restart is a full-platform outage with no in-band recovery lever, and RateLimitService (rate-limit.service.ts:98-105) is the only Redis caller in the request path that actually try/catches.

title: prod-bootstrap.sh treats tenant-schema migration failure as non-fatal — a green deploy can leave live libraries on an old schema
what: `pnpm tenant:migrate || echo "[bootstrap] tenant migrate skipped (non-fatal)"`. The migrate one-shot then exits 0, so compose's `condition: service_completed_successfully` is satisfied and api + worker start against tenant databases that did not receive the new migration. The same pattern is used for the first admin at line 54 (`pnpm admin:bootstrap || echo 'admin bootstrap failed (non-fatal)'`). Only the control-plane migration (line 35) and seed (line 41) are fatal.
impact: Ship a release that adds a tenant column; one library's DB is locked, out of disk, or its credentials rotated; that migration fails; the deploy reports success and the new API code queries a column that does not exist. That library gets 500s on every page while the dashboard is entirely green — nobody finds out until the librarian calls. For line 54: a completely green first deploy that nobody can log into, since the admin was never created (deploy-on-host.sh:75-79 warns only when ADMIN_BOOTSTRAP_EMAIL is empty, not when the bootstrap itself failed).
evidence: READ. scripts/prod-bootstrap.sh lines 49-57 quoted above; the header comment at lines 12-14 states the intent ('best-effort; new tenants self-migrate at signup, and a manual fan-out always exists'), but nothing in the deploy path performs or verifies that manual fan-out. docker-compose.prod.yml:207-209 shows api gated only on `migrate: condition: service_completed_successfully`, which a `|| echo` satisfies. deploy-on-host.sh's health loop asserts container health, never migration coverage.
fix: Make tenant:migrate fatal, or (better) have it exit non-zero and print the failing tenant slugs, and have the deploy either abort or automatically put the affected tenants into `read_only`/`out_of_order` system mode so they fail closed instead of serving broken pages. Make admin:bootstrap fatal on the first deploy (it is idempotent, so a failure always means something is wrong).
verification: Confirmed verbatim against the file. `cat -n scripts/prod-bootstrap.sh` shows lines 34-44 use `if ! pnpm db:migrate:deploy; then ... exit 1; fi` and the same for db:seed, while line 50 is `pnpm tenant:migrate || echo "[bootstrap] tenant migrate skipped (non-fatal)"` and line 54 is `pnpm admin:bootstrap || echo "[bootstrap] admin bootstrap failed (non-fatal)"`; `set -eu` at line 19 is neutralised by the `||`. The underlying script is NOT the sloppy part — scripts/tenant-migrate.ts:120-121 already does `log(... okCount ok, failCount failed)` and `if (failCount > 0) process.exit(2)`, i.e. it deliberately reports per-tenant failure with a distinct exit code that prod-bootstrap.sh then discards. Confirmed the gate: docker-compose.prod.yml:207-209 gates api on `migrate: condition: service_completed_successfully`, which a swallowed failure satisfies, and scripts/deploy-on-host.sh:181 checks only container health (`api=healthy web=healthy worker=healthy`) plus a static Caddy `respond "ok" 200` (infra/caddy/Caddyfile:136-140) — nothing in the gate asserts migration coverage. Searched for a compensating fan-out or drift check in deploy-on-host.sh and .github/workflows/deploy.yml and found none. Severity high upheld: the first deploy has no tenants so tenant:migrate is a no-op, but every release after that can green-light a fleet where one library's schema silently lags the code, and the admin:bootstrap half can produce a fully green FIRST deploy that nobody can log into.

title: The POSTGRES_PASSWORD 'CRITICAL guard' cannot detect a surviving cluster in the very scenario it was written for
what: `pg_data_initialized()` decides whether a Postgres cluster already exists by running `docker volume inspect --format '{{.Mountpoint}}' "${COMPOSE_PROJECT_NAME:-libriant}_pg_data"` and testing for PG_VERSION under that mountpoint. Two things break this in the documented topology. (1) The stated scenario is a 'boot-disk rebuild while the data volume survived' — on Hetzner a rebuild wipes /var/lib/docker, so the named volume's metadata is gone and `docker volume inspect` fails, the function returns 1, and the guard does not fire. (2) Deploys always chain docker-compose.volume.yml (deploy-on-host.sh:105), which redefines pg_data as a `local` driver with `o: bind, device: ${LIBRIANT_DATA_ROOT}/postgres`; the local driver still reports `.Mountpoint` as /var/lib/docker/volumes/<name>/_data, not the bind target, so PG_VERSION is not found there either.
impact: The exact disaster the guard exists to prevent: a fresh boot disk with the data volume still attached, ensure-env.sh mints a brand-new POSTGRES_PASSWORD, writes it to .env.prod, and the Postgres container starts on the surviving PGDATA whose pg_authid still holds the OLD password. Every app connection fails authentication, the stack never comes up, and .env.prod has already been overwritten so the old password is only recoverable from a backup of a file the operator may not have. Total outage with a self-inflicted obstacle to recovery.
evidence: READ (docker is not installed in this audit environment, so the mountpoint behaviour could not be executed here). ensure-env.sh:67-73 quoted; docker-compose.volume.yml:22-28 shows the bind redefinition; deploy-on-host.sh:105 shows both files are always chained; docker-compose.volume.yml:5-6 states the premise 'a server "Rebuild" wipes the boot disk but KEEPS attached volumes'.
fix: Detect the cluster on the filesystem, not through Docker metadata: `[ -f "${LIBRIANT_DATA_ROOT:-/mnt/libriant}/postgres/PG_VERSION" ]` (keeping the docker-volume check as a fallback for non-overlay hosts). Independently, store the generated .env.prod off-host (encrypted) as part of the deploy, so losing the boot disk never loses the password.
verification: Both failure modes confirmed by reading; could not execute (docker is not installed here — `command -v docker` returns nothing). Verified: scripts/ensure-env.sh:67-73 `pg_data_initialized()` requires `command -v docker` and then `docker volume inspect --format '{{.Mountpoint}}' "${COMPOSE_PROJECT_NAME:-libriant}_pg_data"`, testing `[ -f "${mp}/PG_VERSION" ]`; :80-85 is the guard that exits 3. Path (1) holds: infra/compose/docker-compose.volume.yml:5-6 states the premise 'a server "Rebuild" wipes the boot disk but KEEPS attached volumes' — that wipe takes /var/lib/docker with it, so the volume metadata the guard queries no longer exists and the function returns 1 (docker itself may not even be installed yet on the rebuilt disk, tripping the very first line). Path (2) holds: docker-compose.volume.yml:22-28 redefines pg_data as `driver: local` with `o: bind, device: ${LIBRIANT_DATA_ROOT}/postgres`, and deploy-on-host.sh:105 chains BOTH files unconditionally; a local-driver bind volume still reports .Mountpoint as /var/lib/docker/volumes/<name>/_data, which holds no PG_VERSION. I looked for a second, independent guard and found none: ensure-env.sh:96 `ensure_rand POSTGRES_PASSWORD 24` fires the moment the key is absent, and the surviving cluster's pg_authid is not consulted anywhere. deploy-on-host.sh:48/56 only assert the DIRECTORIES exist, which they will. High upheld — this is the failure mode of the documented DR path, and it destroys the recovery material (.env.prod) in the act of failing.

title: Default tenant connection budget is 2.5x Postgres max_connections — the pool config and the DB config in the same repo contradict each other
what: TENANT_CLIENT_CACHE_SIZE defaults to 50 (env.ts:288) and is not set in compose. Each cached tenant client is built by makeTenantPrismaClient with no maxPoolSize override (apps/api/src/tenancy/tenant-prisma.service.ts:72), so it falls back to DEFAULT_TENANT_POOL_MAX = 5 (TENANT_DB_POOL_MAX is never set in compose either). That is 50 x 5 = 250 direct Postgres backends per process, and both `api` and `worker` run this code — up to 500. Tenant URLs are built by swapping the DB name on PG_SUPERUSER_URL (tenant-provisioning.service.ts:104-108), i.e. `postgres:5432` DIRECTLY, bypassing pgbouncer entirely; only the control plane goes through the pooler. Meanwhile the Postgres service is started with `-c max_connections=200`.
impact: At sustained concurrency across roughly 35+ simultaneously-busy tenant databases (api + worker combined) new tenant pool connections get 'FATAL: sorry, too many clients already' on the SHARED Postgres, so the control plane and every other library fail at the same moment, not just the tenant that tripped it. Not reachable at the five-library launch scale; it arrives silently as the customer count and per-library concurrency grow, and nothing asserts the budget anywhere.
evidence: READ. env.ts:288 `tenantClientCacheSize: num('TENANT_CLIENT_CACHE_SIZE', 50, ...)`; packages/db-tenant/src/client.ts:21 `const DEFAULT_TENANT_POOL_MAX = 5;`; tenant-prisma.service.ts:38 `max: env.tenantClientCacheSize`, :72 `makeTenantPrismaClient({ databaseUrl: ctx.dbUrl })` with no maxPoolSize; docker-compose.prod.yml:320-325 `command: [postgres, -c, shared_preload_libraries=..., -c, max_connections=200]`. Cross-check of every process.env read in apps/api + packages against the compose x-app-env block confirms TENANT_CLIENT_CACHE_SIZE and TENANT_DB_POOL_MAX are never injected, so the defaults are what production runs.
fix: Set explicit, arithmetically-consistent values in docker-compose.prod.yml x-app-env: e.g. TENANT_CLIENT_CACHE_SIZE=12 and TENANT_DB_POOL_MAX=3 (12x3x2 processes = 72, leaving headroom under 200 for pgbouncer, the migrate one-shot and psql), or route tenant DBs through pgbouncer too. Additionally assert the budget at boot: fail if tenantClientCacheSize * poolMax * 2 exceeds a configured PG_MAX_CONNECTIONS.
verification: Mechanism confirmed by reading AND measured; impact arithmetic and trigger corrected, so severity drops high -> medium. Verified reads: env.ts:288 `tenantClientCacheSize: num('TENANT_CLIENT_CACHE_SIZE', 50, ...)`; packages/db-tenant/src/client.ts:21 `const DEFAULT_TENANT_POOL_MAX = 5;` and :56 `new PrismaPg({connectionString, max: resolveMaxPoolSize(...)})`; tenant-prisma.service.ts:72 passes no maxPoolSize; `grep -n TENANT_ infra/compose/docker-compose.prod.yml` returns ONLY line 46 TENANT_PATH_PREFIX, so both defaults do ship; compose:324 `-c max_connections=200`; provisioning path is apps/api/src/provisioning/tenant-provisioning.service.ts:104-108 (the original 'where' cited apps/api/src/tenancy/..., which does not exist) and it does swap the DB name on PG_SUPERUSER_URL, which compose:87 points at `postgres:5432` directly, bypassing pgbouncer. EXECUTED a pool probe against the audit Postgres (10 clients from makeTenantPrismaClient, 5 concurrent queries each, backend count read from pg_stat_activity): 'after constructing 10 clients (no query): 0' / 'right after 10x5 concurrent burst: 50' / '2s later: 50' / '15s later (idle): 0'. So connections are opened lazily and node-postgres reaps them after ~10s idle. CORRECTION to the finding: the ceiling is driven by PEAK CONCURRENCY, not by how many libraries are cached — an idle cached client holds zero backends. Exhaustion needs ~35 tenants (200 minus pgbouncer's DEFAULT_POOL_SIZE=20 and superuser reserve, divided by 5) each with 5 in-flight queries at the same instant, across api+worker. The launch posture is five pilot libraries, so this cannot fire on Monday; it is a growth-time cliff, not a release blocker. The 250-vs-200 contradiction between two files in one repo is real and worth fixing before the fleet grows.

title: ensure-env.sh writes EMAIL_DRIVER=console on every deploy, permanently defeating the compose fail-fast that was deliberately added to prevent exactly that
what: docker-compose.prod.yml deliberately passes EMAIL_DRIVER through unset (`EMAIL_DRIVER: ${EMAIL_DRIVER:-}`) with a comment (REL-06) explaining that a `:-console` default was removed because it 'silently DISABLED the fail-fast env.ts builds in for production', and that 'an operator who forgets gets the loud env.ts boot-time failure rather than silent, PII-logging email'. But scripts/ensure-env.sh:101 does `ensure_default EMAIL_DRIVER console`, and ensure-env.sh --auto runs on EVERY deploy (deploy-on-host.sh:97, .github/workflows/deploy.yml:281) before compose reads the file. So .env.prod always contains EMAIL_DRIVER=console and the loud failure the compose file promises is unreachable — including for an operator who deliberately deletes the line to get it.
impact: No email is ever delivered in production and nothing at boot says so. Password reset, email verification, support-key delivery and announcement mail all silently no-op; the outbox row is marked sent with a fabricated `console-<hex>` providerId, so even the admin view says delivered. A librarian who forgets her password has no self-service recovery path and no error to report. Two files in the same deploy path assert opposite policies, which means whichever one a future operator reads, they will be wrong.
evidence: EXECUTED + READ. Executed: booting with EMAIL_DRIVER set to empty (the exact value compose injects) under NODE_ENV=production exits 1 with `Error: EMAIL_DRIVER=smtp requires SMTP_URL (e.g. smtp://user:pass@host:587).` at smtp-driver.ts:27 — i.e. the compose fail-fast works, and is the only thing standing between a fresh host and a crash-loop. Read: ensure-env.sh:62 `ensure_default() { ... [ -n "$(getv ...)" ] || setv ... }` and :101 `ensure_default EMAIL_DRIVER console`; deploy-on-host.sh:97 `bash scripts/ensure-env.sh --auto "$ENV_FILE"`. console-driver.ts:31-36 confirms the non-dev branch only logs 'NOT delivering ... (body withheld)' at warn level.
fix: Delete the `ensure_default EMAIL_DRIVER console` line so the compose contract holds, and instead have ensure-env.sh prompt for (or require) a real driver. If a console-only launch is genuinely intended, make it explicit and loud: log an ERROR-level line at boot naming every feature that is disabled, and surface a persistent banner in the admin panel.
verification: Contradiction confirmed; impact partly overstated and partly restates the brief's known state, so severity drops high -> medium. Verified: docker-compose.prod.yml:69-77 carries the REL-06 comment and `EMAIL_DRIVER: ${EMAIL_DRIVER:-}` (pass-through unset, deliberately no `:-console`); scripts/ensure-env.sh:62 `ensure_default() { ... [ -n "$(getv "${k}")" ] || setv ... }` and :101 `ensure_default EMAIL_DRIVER console`; scripts/deploy-on-host.sh:97 and .github/workflows/deploy.yml:281 both run `bash scripts/ensure-env.sh --auto` before compose. So the loud boot failure the compose comment promises is indeed unreachable on any host these scripts touch, and an operator who deletes the line gets it re-added on the next deploy. Two files in one deploy path do assert opposite policies. CORRECTION: 'nothing says so' is only true of BOOT — console-driver.ts:30-35 logs a per-send WARN in every non-dev environment ("NOT delivering \"<subject>\" to <to> (body withheld). Configure EMAIL_DRIVER=resend|smtp to actually send."), so the condition is observable in the logs on every attempted send, and the same code path means reset TOKENS are NOT written to prod logs (contrary to the audit brief's own known-state note). The remaining harm — outbox rows marked sent with a fabricated `console-<hex>` providerId (console-driver.ts:24,37) so the admin view reads as delivered, and no self-service password recovery — is real but is also the deliberate, known launch posture rather than an accident.

title: The web container's healthcheck cannot fail while the API is down, and the deploy gate trusts it
what: The web service healthcheck is `wget -qO- http://localhost:3000/api/healthz`. That route returns a constant `{status:'ok'}` and, by its own comment, 'Doesn't touch the API or any other dependency'. A `/api/readyz` route already exists that fetches the API's /readyz over the docker network — it is not used by any probe. deploy-on-host.sh:181 gates the deploy on `web=healthy`, and web's own `depends_on: api: condition: service_healthy` only covers the initial start ordering, not steady state.
impact: A wrong API_INTERNAL_URL or a broken `app` network is invisible: web reports healthy, all four deploy-gate signals go green, and every page a librarian opens renders an error. In steady state the web container can never transition to unhealthy however badly the API is behaving, so the container-health dashboard is permanently green for the web tier. (A fully dead api container IS caught at deploy time by the `api=healthy` check — that half of the original impact does not hold.)
evidence: READ. docker-compose.prod.yml:259-264 (`test: ['CMD','wget','-qO-','http://localhost:3000/api/healthz']`); apps/web/app/api/healthz/route.ts:3-14; apps/web/app/api/readyz/route.ts:22 (`await fetch(\`${apiBase}/readyz\`)`); deploy-on-host.sh:181 (`[ "$web" = "healthy" ]`).
fix: Point the web healthcheck at /api/readyz (keeping /api/healthz for a pure liveness probe), and make the deploy gate additionally curl one real page through Caddy rather than only asserting container health.
verification: Confirmed, with the impact tightened. Verified: docker-compose.prod.yml:259-264 `test: ['CMD','wget','-qO-','http://localhost:3000/api/healthz']`; apps/web/app/api/healthz/route.ts:13-15 returns a constant `{status:'ok', bootedAt}` and its comment says "Doesn't touch the API or any other dependency"; apps/web/app/api/readyz/route.ts:12-45 already fetches `${API_INTERNAL_URL}/readyz` with a 3s AbortController and returns 503 — and `grep` shows no probe anywhere references it. CORRECTION to the finding's impact: the deploy gate is NOT blind to a dead API — deploy-on-host.sh:181 requires `api=healthy`, and the api healthcheck (compose:223) is the deep `/readyz`. The real residual is narrower but still real: the gate's four signals are `edge` (Caddy's own static `respond "ok" 200` at infra/caddy/Caddyfile:136-140 — proves nothing about any app), `site` (the marketing-site vhost), `api=healthy`, and `web=healthy` (the constant). Not one of them ever renders a real panel page or crosses the web->api hop, so a wrong API_INTERNAL_URL or a broken `app` network passes the gate with everything green, and in steady state web can never go unhealthy no matter what happens behind it. Medium upheld.

title: NODE_ENV is cast, never validated — a typo silently un-gates the dev-only smoke-test controller, honours RATE_LIMIT_DISABLED, and collapses STORAGE_SIGNING_SECRET into SESSION_SECRET
what: `const nodeEnv = (process.env.NODE_ENV ?? 'development') as AppEnv['nodeEnv'];` — a bare cast with no allow-list. Four separate protections key on the string being EXACTLY 'production': main.ts:15 (refuse to boot with RATE_LIMIT_DISABLED=true), platform/rate-limit.service.ts:67 (ignore the flag), plans/plan-demo.controller.ts:45 (NonProductionOnlyGuard), env.ts:344 (require STORAGE_SIGNING_SECRET rather than defaulting it to sessionSecret). Anything else — 'Production', 'prod', 'staging' — is neither dev (so the secrets are still demanded, making it look correctly configured) nor production (so all four protections switch off). And with NODE_ENV unset entirely the process boots with the committed dev fallbacks for SESSION_SECRET, ADMIN_SESSION_SECRET, IMPERSONATION_SECRET, MFA_MASTER_KEY and HASH_PEPPER.
impact: No impact on the Monday release: NODE_ENV is pinned to 'production' by both apps/api/Dockerfile:83 and the literal at docker-compose.prod.yml:35, and .env.prod cannot override it. The residual is latent: the day someone stands up a second cell with NODE_ENV=staging, the dev-only PlanDemoController (whose own header says POST /demo/books 'performs a REAL, unvalidated book write that bypasses the race-safe quota authority') becomes reachable, RATE_LIMIT_DISABLED starts being honoured, and STORAGE_SIGNING_SECRET silently falls back to SESSION_SECRET.
evidence: EXECUTED. Booted the API against the live audit env and probed a real seeded tenant slug. NODE_ENV=production: `GET /t/probes1-x9/plan` → 404, `/plan/usage` → 404 (NonProductionOnlyGuard firing). NODE_ENV=Production: → 401, 401. NODE_ENV=staging: → 401, 401 (guard passed; only authentication is left). Also executed: `NODE_ENV=Production` with STORAGE_SIGNING_SECRET unset → RESULT: BOOTED_OK readyz=200 (production refuses: 'Missing required env var: STORAGE_SIGNING_SECRET'). Also executed: `NODE_ENV=staging RATE_LIMIT_DISABLED=true` → BOOTED_OK (production exits 1 with 'refusing to boot'). Also executed: NODE_ENV unset with SESSION_SECRET/ADMIN_SESSION_SECRET/IMPERSONATION_SECRET/MFA_MASTER_KEY/HASH_PEPPER/STORAGE_SIGNING_SECRET all unset → RESULT: BOOTED_OK readyz=200.
fix: In loadEnv(), validate: `const raw = process.env.NODE_ENV; if (raw !== undefined && !['development','production','test'].includes(raw)) throw new Error(...)`. Better still, require NODE_ENV to be set explicitly outside of local dev rather than defaulting to 'development'. Then replace the `!== 'production'` checks with a single `isProduction` derived once.
verification: Mechanism confirmed, stated impact REFUTED for the shipped deploy path; severity drops high -> low. env.ts:223 is indeed a bare cast (`const nodeEnv = (process.env.NODE_ENV ?? 'development') as AppEnv['nodeEnv'];`) with no allow-list, and the four `=== 'production'` / `!== 'production'` checks are where the finding says (main.ts:15, rate-limit.service.ts:67, plan-demo.controller.ts:45, env.ts:344). BUT the guard the auditor did not look for is that NODE_ENV is never operator-supplied: `grep -n NODE_ENV infra/compose/docker-compose.prod.yml apps/api/Dockerfile scripts/ensure-env.sh scripts/deploy-on-host.sh` gives apps/api/Dockerfile:83 `ENV NODE_ENV=production`, docker-compose.prod.yml:35 `NODE_ENV: production` (a LITERAL inside x-app-env, not `${NODE_ENV:-...}`) and :240 the same for web. ensure-env.sh never writes NODE_ENV, so nothing in .env.prod can override it — Compose's literal wins over the image ENV and both say `production`. Therefore 'NODE_ENV unset -> committed dev secrets' and "NODE_ENV='staging' -> PlanDemoController reachable / RATE_LIMIT_DISABLED honoured / STORAGE_SIGNING_SECRET collapses into SESSION_SECRET" cannot occur in any deployment this repo produces; the auditor reached them only by setting NODE_ENV by hand outside the deploy path. Note also that under 'staging' requiredSecret() still takes the non-dev branch, so the secrets are still demanded, and cookieSecure (env.ts:255) already special-cases 'any env other than development/test'. What survives is a genuine hardening gap with defence-in-depth value if a staging cell is ever added.

title: CONTROL_DATABASE_URL, REDIS_URL, PG_SUPERUSER_URL and STORAGE_ROOT are optional() with production-shaped localhost defaults; a missing PG_SUPERUSER_URL boots fully green
what: Four values the app cannot function without are read with `optional()` and a hard-coded fallback: CONTROL_DATABASE_URL → `postgresql://libriant:libriant@localhost:5432/libriant_control`, REDIS_URL → `redis://localhost:6379`, PG_SUPERUSER_URL → the same localhost superuser URL with credentials `libriant:libriant`, STORAGE_ROOT → `/srv/libriant/storage`. The file's own header says 'every value we depend on is either present + valid, or boot fails loudly'; these four are the exceptions. PG_SUPERUSER_URL is the worst case because nothing in the startup or readiness path touches it — it is only used at tenant-signup time to CREATE DATABASE and to derive every tenant's connection URL.
impact: No production path can reach the fallbacks — compose hard-codes all four. The residual is defence-in-depth: anything running the API outside compose (a host-level `pnpm start`, a future non-compose orchestrator, a one-off script) silently gets localhost URLs and the guessable libriant/libriant superuser credentials instead of a loud failure, and PG_SUPERUSER_URL specifically is touched by nothing in the startup or readiness path so the mistake would only surface at the first tenant signup.
evidence: EXECUTED, one variable at a time, NODE_ENV=production against the live audit Postgres/Redis. `unset PG_SUPERUSER_URL` → RESULT: BOOTED_OK readyz=200. `unset STORAGE_ROOT` → RESULT: BOOTED_OK readyz=200. `unset CONTROL_DATABASE_URL` → RESULT: BOOTED_OK readyz=503. `unset REDIS_URL` → RESULT: BOOTED_OK readyz=500. By contrast every secret fails loudly: SESSION_SECRET / ADMIN_SESSION_SECRET / IMPERSONATION_SECRET / MFA_MASTER_KEY / HASH_PEPPER / STORAGE_SIGNING_SECRET each exit rc=1 with 'Missing required env var: <NAME>'.
fix: Make all four `required()` when nodeEnv !== 'development'. Keep the localhost strings as dev-only fallbacks the same way the secrets do it. For STORAGE_ROOT additionally assert at boot that the directory exists and is writable (see boot-and-config-12).
verification: Code claim confirmed, stated impact REFUTED for the deploy path; severity drops medium -> low. env.ts:265-270 and :334-337 do use optional() with those exact production-shaped localhost fallbacks, and I reproduced the fail-loud contrast (unset SESSION_SECRET -> 'Missing required env var: SESSION_SECRET', unset STORAGE_SIGNING_SECRET -> same, PORT=abc -> 'must be a number', MFA_MASTER_KEY=deadbeef -> 'must be 64 hex characters'). But the guard the auditor missed is that all four are LITERALS in the compose env block, not operator-supplied: `grep -n 'PG_SUPERUSER_URL|STORAGE_ROOT|CONTROL_DATABASE_URL|REDIS_URL' infra/compose/docker-compose.prod.yml` gives :36 CONTROL_DATABASE_URL, :37 `REDIS_URL: redis://redis:6379`, :52 `STORAGE_ROOT: /srv/libriant/storage`, :87 PG_SUPERUSER_URL — none of them `${...}`-optional except the embedded ${POSTGRES_PASSWORD}, which is itself `:?POSTGRES_PASSWORD is required` at :317 and :344, so compose aborts the whole `up` rather than interpolating empty. The headline scenario — 'a missing PG_SUPERUSER_URL boots fully green and then does DDL against localhost with libriant/libriant at first signup' — therefore has no path through any deployment this repo produces, including the bare `docker compose -f docker-compose.prod.yml up -d` at compose:16, which still applies x-app-env. What remains is a real but purely defensive inconsistency with the file's own 'present + valid, or boot fails loudly' header.

title: PUBLIC_HOST's default disagrees between two blocks of the same compose file and the Caddyfile — an unset value points the browser's API base at the marketing site
where: infra/compose/docker-compose.prod.yml:38 and :68 and :247-248 (default `libriant.com`) vs :141 and infra/caddy/Caddyfile:149 (default `app.libriant.com`)
what: x-app-env builds `PUBLIC_APP_URL: https://${PUBLIC_HOST:-libriant.com}` and `BILLING_RETURN_URL` the same way; the web service gets `NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL: https://${PUBLIC_HOST:-libriant.com}`. The caddy service block and the Caddyfile both default the same variable to `app.libriant.com`, and ensure-env.sh:105 writes `PUBLIC_HOST=app.libriant.com`. So with PUBLIC_HOST unset, Caddy serves the app vhost at app.libriant.com while the app and the browser bundle believe the app lives at libriant.com — which is the SITE_HOST vhost (Caddyfile:253), a marketing-site vhost that proxies only /apply to the API.
impact: Browser-side calls to https://libriant.com/lbr-api/* land on the marketing vhost and 404; the panel loads its shell and then fails on every data fetch. Password-reset and billing-return links point at the marketing site. Every container healthcheck stays green throughout. The compose file's own header (line 16) documents `docker compose -f infra/compose/docker-compose.prod.yml up -d` as a valid way to bring the stack up — that invocation, with a partially-populated env file, produces exactly this.
evidence: READ. docker-compose.prod.yml:38 `PUBLIC_APP_URL: https://${PUBLIC_HOST:-libriant.com}`, :141 `PUBLIC_HOST: ${PUBLIC_HOST:-app.libriant.com}`, :247 `NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL: https://${PUBLIC_HOST:-libriant.com}`; infra/caddy/Caddyfile:149 `{$PUBLIC_HOST:app.libriant.com}` vs :253 `{$SITE_HOST:libriant.com}`; scripts/ensure-env.sh:105 `ensure_default PUBLIC_HOST app.libriant.com`.
fix: Make PUBLIC_HOST mandatory in compose (`${PUBLIC_HOST:?PUBLIC_HOST is required}`), exactly as SESSION_SECRET and HASH_PEPPER already are — there is no safe default for it now that the app and the site are different hosts.
verification: Contradiction confirmed exactly; reachability is narrower than stated, so severity drops medium -> low. Verified line by line: docker-compose.prod.yml:38 `PUBLIC_APP_URL: https://${PUBLIC_HOST:-libriant.com}`, :68 `BILLING_RETURN_URL: https://${PUBLIC_HOST:-libriant.com}`, :247-248 `NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL`/`PUBLIC_APP_URL: https://${PUBLIC_HOST:-libriant.com}` versus :141 `PUBLIC_HOST: ${PUBLIC_HOST:-app.libriant.com}` in the caddy block and infra/caddy/Caddyfile:149 `{$PUBLIC_HOST:app.libriant.com}` / :253 `{$SITE_HOST:libriant.com}`. The consequence is also confirmed: Caddyfile:247-250 documents that the SITE_HOST vhost deliberately has NO `handle_path /lbr-api/*` block, so browser calls to https://libriant.com/lbr-api/* really would 404. BUT the value is set on every real deploy — scripts/ensure-env.sh:105 `ensure_default PUBLIC_HOST app.libriant.com`, and ensure-env.sh --auto runs before compose in both deploy paths (deploy-on-host.sh:97, .github/workflows/deploy.yml:281). Reaching the bad default requires bringing the stack up by hand, bypassing ensure-env.sh, with an env file complete enough to satisfy the five `:?`-required secrets yet missing PUBLIC_HOST. That is a real trap for a future operator but not a Monday failure mode.

title: Billing flags are not cross-validated and are not echoed at boot: BILLING_ENABLED=true with STRIPE_DRIVER=fake starts silently, and BILLING_ENABLED='enabled' silently means false
what: billingEnabled and stripeDriver are resolved independently with no consistency check. `BILLING_ENABLED=true` + `STRIPE_DRIVER=fake` boots with plan/quota enforcement ON and the in-memory FakeStripeDriver behind every checkout and portal call, with no warning logged. Separately, bool() accepts only true/1/yes/on (case-insensitive), so a plausible operator value such as `BILLING_ENABLED=enabled` or `=y` resolves to false — i.e. the entire product becomes free — again with nothing logged.
impact: Not a fleet-wide silent-free-tier risk — the platform_settings row overrides env and the launch default is false either way. The real residual: enforcement can be switched on (via BILLING_ENABLED=true in .env.prod OR via the admin Subscriptions toggle) while STRIPE_DRIVER is still `fake`, with nothing in either path warning, so plan limits are enforced against paying customers whose checkout and portal calls go to the in-memory FakeStripeDriver and collect no money.
evidence: EXECUTED. Booted with BILLING_ENABLED=true STRIPE_DRIVER=fake under NODE_ENV=production → RESULT: BOOTED_OK readyz=200; `grep -ci warn` over the full boot log returned 0, and no log line mentions billing state, the resolved Stripe driver, or the email driver. Also executed: BILLING_ENABLED=TRUE → boots (lower-cased to true); BILLING_ENABLED=enabled → boots, silently false. The only boot line the process emits about its configuration is main.ts:61 `[libriant-api] listening on :3001 (production)`.
fix: In loadEnv(), throw when billingEnabled && stripeDriver === 'fake' outside development. Make bool() reject any value that is not in a known true/false allow-list rather than silently treating unknown strings as false. And log one INFO line at boot with the resolved effective configuration (nodeEnv, emailDriver, stripeDriver, billingEnabled, adminMfaRequired, sessionCookieSecure, control DB host, redis host, storageRoot) — no secrets.
verification: Two of the three sub-claims survive only weakly; the headline impact is REFUTED by a guard the auditor did not find, so severity drops medium -> low. The env resolution is as described (env.ts:214-218 bool() accepts only true/1/yes/on; :366 `billingEnabled: bool('BILLING_ENABLED', false)`; :352-359 stripeDriver resolved independently). BUT env.BILLING_ENABLED is NOT the switch: apps/api/src/platform-settings/platform-settings.service.ts:32-39 reads a platform_settings DB row and only falls back to `loadEnv().billingEnabled` when the row is absent (`const value = row ? row.value === 'true' : loadEnv().billingEnabled;`), and every consumer goes through it — effective-plan.service.ts:110, billing.service.ts:130/162/178, desktop.controller.ts:50. env.ts:361-363 says so in a comment the finding quoted around. The authoritative control is the owner-only admin toggle at platform-settings/admin-subscriptions.controller.ts:34-56, which audit-logs the change. So "BILLING_ENABLED='enabled' silently means false and removes every plan limit across the fleet" does not hold: the default is false anyway, and once anyone touches the admin toggle the env var is inert. What survives is genuine: nothing cross-validates enforcement-on against STRIPE_DRIVER=fake — and note this is reachable through the ADMIN TOGGLE too, not just env, since admin-subscriptions.controller.ts:34-56 checks nothing about the resolved driver before flipping enforcement on. The third sub-claim (no boot-time echo of resolved configuration) is an observability preference, not a defect.

title: /readyz's per-dependency detail is swallowed by the global exception filter, so the readiness probe cannot say what is broken
what: readiness() builds `{status, dependencies: {redis, controlDb}}` and throws it as a ServiceUnavailableException. The global HttpExceptionFilter re-skins 5xx responses into a generic envelope, so the body the operator actually receives is `{"statusCode":503,"error":"InternalServerError","message":"Sorry — something went wrong on our end...","supportCode":"..."}` — the dependencies map is gone. Related: compose uses `restart: unless-stopped`, which does not restart a container merely because its healthcheck is failing, so an api stuck 'unhealthy' stays up serving errors indefinitely.
impact: The probe response is diagnostically useless and mislabels a dependency outage as InternalServerError, so an operator reading only the HTTP body cannot tell Postgres from Redis. Cost is one extra log grep (the dependency map is already logged against the same supportCode), not an inability to diagnose.
evidence: EXECUTED. With CONTROL_DATABASE_URL pointed at a dead port: `curl /readyz` → `{"statusCode":503,"error":"InternalServerError","message":"Sorry — something went wrong on our end. We've logged it. Please try again, or send us this code if it keeps happening: CIOW15V0","supportCode":"CIOW15V0"}` [503]. The `dependencies` object built at health.controller.ts:44 never reaches the client.
fix: Exempt /healthz, /readyz and /metrics from HttpExceptionFilter (or return the 503 body directly with res.status(503).json(body) instead of throwing), so the probe response carries the dependency map.
verification: Mechanism reproduced; impact materially overstated, so severity drops medium -> low. RE-EXECUTED: booted with CONTROL_DATABASE_URL pointed at dead port 55999 and Redis alive. `curl /healthz` -> 200 `{"status":"ok",...}`; `curl /readyz` -> 503 `{"statusCode":503,"error":"InternalServerError","message":"Sorry — something went wrong...","supportCode":"C88WNULU"}` — the `dependencies` map is indeed absent from the client body, and the label really does say InternalServerError for a dependency outage. BUT the claim that the operator 'has to shell into the container and read logs' understates what the logs already give: http-exception.filter.ts:80-99 logs `declaredBody` on the SAME one-line JSON record as the supportCode, and I grepped it out of the run: `declaredBody":{"status":"not_ready","dependencies":{"redis":true,"controlDb":false}}`. So the dependency map IS emitted to stdout, greppable by the support code the caller already has — a `docker compose logs api | grep C88WNULU` away, not a debugging dead end. The mislabelled `error` field and the lost probe body remain real papercuts worth the one-line fix. The `restart: unless-stopped` sub-remark is accurate but is a separate observation, not part of this defect.

title: The web container mounts locales at /srv/libriant/locales but is never told where they are — the mount is inert and the legal/i18n content depends on an unverified in-image path
what: x-app-env sets `LOCALES_ROOT: /srv/libriant/locales` for api/worker/migrate. The web service defines its own environment block (compose merges nothing into it) and omits LOCALES_ROOT, while still bind-mounting `../../locales:/srv/libriant/locales:ro`. apps/web/lib/locale-loader.ts:9 and apps/web/lib/legal.ts:21 both do `process.env.LOCALES_ROOT?.trim() || REPO_LOCALES`, where REPO_LOCALES is `path.resolve(dirname(fileURLToPath(import.meta.url)), '..','..','..','locales')` — a path resolved relative to the compiled server chunk, not to the source file.
impact: The read-only locales mount does nothing for the web container: editing /srv/libriant/locales on the host changes no rendered string or legal document. All localized copy and all seven legal documents are served from whatever REPO_LOCALES happens to resolve to inside the built image; if that resolution moves with a Next build-output change, the legal pages 404 and the i18n loader throws on a file read, with no configuration knob to correct it. The same code in the API is protected by LOCALES_ROOT; web is not.
evidence: READ. docker-compose.prod.yml:55 vs the web block at :239-251 (no LOCALES_ROOT) and its volumes at :255-257 (`../../locales:/srv/libriant/locales:ro`); apps/web/lib/locale-loader.ts:7-9; apps/web/lib/legal.ts:19-21; apps/web/Dockerfile copies `locales` into /app at build time, so the in-image copy is at /app/locales.
fix: Add `LOCALES_ROOT: /srv/libriant/locales` (and ASSETS_ROOT, which the web service also mounts but does not declare) to the web service's environment block, so both containers resolve content the same way and the bind mount is real.
verification: Confirmed as written, with one speculative clause disproved. Verified: docker-compose.prod.yml:55 sets `LOCALES_ROOT: /srv/libriant/locales` in x-app-env (api/worker/migrate only); the web service at :239-253 declares its own `environment:` block with NODE_ENV/PORT/NEXT_TELEMETRY_DISABLED/API_INTERNAL_URL/NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL/PUBLIC_APP_URL/ADMIN_HOST and no LOCALES_ROOT or ASSETS_ROOT, while :255-257 bind-mounts `../../locales:/srv/libriant/locales:ro` and `../../assets:/srv/libriant/assets:ro`. apps/web/lib/locale-loader.ts:7-9 and apps/web/lib/legal.ts:19-21 both fall back to REPO_LOCALES. So the two read-only mounts on the web container are genuinely inert. DISPROVED the finding's speculative half: I inspected the actual build output (apps/web/.next/server/chunks/'[root-of-the-server]__1913mvv._.js') and Turbopack preserves the SOURCE path in the runtime module URL — `fileURLToPath({get url(){return e.F("apps/web/lib/locale-loader.ts")}}.url)` — so REPO_LOCALES resolves to <root>/locales, i.e. /app/locales, which apps/web/Dockerfile:40 does populate. Content is served correctly today; the fear that a build-output change silently 404s the legal pages is a possibility, not a present defect. Low upheld: the concrete harm is that editing /srv/libriant/locales on the host changes nothing for web, and web and api can drift apart because only one of them honours the mount.

title: Postgres is started with LANG=el_GR.UTF-8 on an Alpine (musl) image that has no such locale
what: `LANG: el_GR.UTF-8` is set on the postgres service. The alpine variant is built against musl, which ships no locale definitions; setlocale() accepts any name and behaves as C. initdb therefore records lc_collate/lc_ctype as el_GR.UTF-8 in pg_control while the actual collation behaviour is byte order.
impact: Two consequences. Greek text ordering (ORDER BY on titles, author names, member surnames) is byte order rather than Greek collation, so accented and uppercase forms sort wrongly in a product whose entire market is Greek libraries. More seriously, the cluster carries a collation label that is a lie: if the data directory or a base backup is ever brought up on a glibc-based Postgres — a plausible DR or migration path — the recorded collation becomes real and every text btree index built under the C behaviour is silently inconsistent with it, which is the classic collation-change index-corruption scenario.
evidence: READ (docker is not installed in this audit environment, so initdb's behaviour on this exact image could not be executed). docker-compose.prod.yml:306-319; the audit environment's own setup script sidesteps the question by using `--locale=C` (docs/audit/pre-release-2026-08-23/env/setup-audit-env.sh:22), so no local cluster reproduces the production locale.
fix: Either move to the Debian-based `postgres:16` image and keep el_GR.UTF-8 (locales are generated there), or drop LANG and initdb with `--locale-provider=icu --icu-locale=el-GR` so the collation is provided by ICU rather than the C library and travels with the data. Decide before the first real cluster is created — this cannot be changed in place without a reindex.
verification: Could not execute — `command -v docker` returns nothing on this machine, so initdb's behaviour on postgres:16-alpine was not observed; this stays a read-only finding and its 'medium' confidence is the right label. Verified the facts that are checkable here: docker-compose.prod.yml:307 `image: postgres:16-alpine` and :319 `LANG: el_GR.UTF-8` in the postgres service environment, with the cluster created by the entrypoint's initdb on first start; the audit environment's own bootstrap sidesteps the question (docs/audit/pre-release-2026-08-23/env/setup-audit-env.sh:22 passes `--locale=C`), so nothing in this repo exercises the production locale. The reasoning stands on a property of the image rather than of this code — musl ships no locale definitions, so the name is accepted and behaves as C — and the two consequences (byte-order sorting for Greek titles/author names/member surnames in a Greek-only product, and a pg_control collation label that becomes real and index-inconsistent if the data directory or a base backup is ever restored onto a glibc Postgres) both follow. Low upheld, but flagged as decide-before-first-cluster: it cannot be changed in place without a full reindex.

title: The pgbouncer healthcheck proves only that the pooler accepts connections, and nothing depends on it being healthy anyway
what: `pg_isready -h localhost -p 5432 -U libriant` against pgbouncer. pg_isready reports 'accepting connections' as soon as the pooler answers a startup packet — it never reaches Postgres, so the probe passes while the backend behind the pool is unreachable. Meanwhile api declares `pgbouncer: condition: service_started`, not service_healthy, so the health status is not consumed by anything.
impact: The one component the control plane's every query passes through has a healthcheck that cannot go red for the failure that matters, and a result nothing reads. Diagnosing a control-plane outage starts one step further back than it should. (The api's own /readyz does catch the resulting failure, which is why this is low rather than higher.)
evidence: READ. docker-compose.prod.yml:355-359 and :207-215; x-app-env:36 routes CONTROL_DATABASE_URL through `pgbouncer:5432`.
fix: Probe through the pooler to the backend, e.g. `psql "postgresql://libriant:$DB_PASSWORD@localhost:5432/libriant_control" -c 'select 1'`, and change api's depends_on to `pgbouncer: condition: service_healthy`.
verification: Confirmed, and it is as inconsequential as the finding itself concedes. Verified: docker-compose.prod.yml:355-359 `test: ['CMD-SHELL','pg_isready -h localhost -p 5432 -U libriant']` on the pgbouncer service (pgbouncer answers the startup packet itself, so this never reaches Postgres); :210-211 `pgbouncer: condition: service_started` in api's depends_on, so nothing consumes the health status; :36 routes CONTROL_DATABASE_URL through `pgbouncer:5432`. Also checked the deploy gate — deploy-on-host.sh:181 asserts api/web/worker only, never pgbouncer — which confirms the status is read by nothing at all. Kept at low rather than promoted or dropped: the api's own deep `/readyz` (compose:223) does catch the underlying failure, so the only cost is that `docker compose ps` shows a green pooler during a control-plane outage. One-line fix, near-zero risk of it ever waking anyone up.

title: What the boot matrix confirmed IS correct — the fail-loud paths that work
what: For completeness of the negative result: every one of these was executed against the live audit environment under NODE_ENV=production and produced a clear, immediate, non-zero exit with a named variable in the message — no silent degradation.
impact: None. Recorded so the orchestrator knows the enumeration was exhaustive and the remaining findings are the exceptions, not the rule.
evidence: EXECUTED, one boot per case. Missing → exit 1 with 'Missing required env var: <NAME>': SESSION_SECRET, ADMIN_SESSION_SECRET, IMPERSONATION_SECRET, MFA_MASTER_KEY, HASH_PEPPER, STORAGE_SIGNING_SECRET. Malformed → exit 1 with a precise message: PORT=abc ('Env var PORT must be a number, got "abc".'), MFA_MASTER_KEY=deadbeef ('must be 64 hex characters (a 32-byte key)'), SESSION_SECRET=shortkey ('is too short — needs at least 24 characters'). Driver misconfiguration → exit 1 at Nest module init: EMAIL_DRIVER resolving to smtp without SMTP_URL, STRIPE_DRIVER resolving to real without STRIPE_API_KEY. Escape hatch → exit 1: RATE_LIMIT_DISABLED=true under NODE_ENV=production. A cross-check of every `process.env.*` read in apps/api + packages against the compose x-app-env block found no env.ts key missing from compose (the two reads outside env.ts that compose does not inject are TENANT_DB_POOL_MAX — see boot-and-config-02 — and WORKER_PORT, which the worker service does set).
fix: No change needed. Preserve these behaviours when fixing boot-and-config-07 by extending the same `required()` treatment to the four remaining optional() infrastructure URLs.
verification: Spot-checked five of the enumerated cases by re-executing them under NODE_ENV=production against the live audit environment; all five reproduced exactly: `unset SESSION_SECRET` -> 'Missing required env var: SESSION_SECRET'; `unset STORAGE_SIGNING_SECRET` -> 'Missing required env var: STORAGE_SIGNING_SECRET'; `PORT=abc` -> 'Env var PORT must be a number, got "abc".'; `MFA_MASTER_KEY=deadbeef` -> 'Env var MFA_MASTER_KEY must be 64 hex characters (a 32-byte key).'; `RATE_LIMIT_DISABLED=true` -> 'refusing to boot'. Each exited non-zero without listening. Also independently re-derived the compose cross-check the entry claims and found it slightly UNDERSTATED in the app's favour: NODE_ENV, CONTROL_DATABASE_URL, REDIS_URL, STORAGE_ROOT and PG_SUPERUSER_URL are all hard literals in x-app-env (compose:35,36,37,52,87), which is what removes the teeth from boot-and-config-03 and -07. Retained as an accurate negative result.
